questions.prompt: How do the primers used in PCR differ from the primers a cell uses in DNA replication?

options.text: PCR primers are made of RNA by primase in the tube; a cell's primers are short DNA stretches made by polymerase
PCR primers bind anywhere on the DNA at random; a cell's primers bind only at the origin of replication
PCR primers are short DNA stretches made in the lab and chosen to flank the target; a cell's primers are RNA laid down by primase
PCR primers are made of protein that holds the strands apart; a cell's primers are made of RNA

questions.explanation: Mullis built short stretches of DNA matching the letters that flank the region to copy. In cells, primase makes RNA primers.

questions.prompt: Each PCR cycle roughly doubles the target. Starting from one target molecule, about how many copies are there after 10 cycles?

options.text: About 10 (one new copy per cycle)
About 20 (2 copies per cycle × 10 cycles)
About 1,000 (2 to the 10th power = 1,024)

questions.prompt: Why doesn't binary fission count as horizontal gene transfer?

options.text: It is cloning — it passes identical genetic information to the next generation rather than swapping genes with a neighbor
It copies only the plasmids, never the chromosome, so no genes are actually passed along to the new cell
It mixes genes from two parent cells into each daughter cell, which makes it a form of vertical transfer
It needs restriction enzymes to cut the chromosome in half, and bacteria can only get those from scientists

questions.explanation: Lecture: binary fission 'is just cloning.' Horizontal transfer = exchanging genetic information with neighbors within a generation.

questions.prompt: Why did genetic engineering in bacteria focus on plasmids rather than the bacterial chromosome?

options.text: Plasmids are made of RNA, so a gene placed in one can be translated right away without being transcribed first
Plasmids hold all of the bacterium's essential genes, so editing a plasmid changes every trait the cell has
Plasmids are the only DNA in a bacterium that restriction enzymes can't cut, so a gene placed there is protected from damage
Plasmids are small, separate loops of 'bonus' genes that bacteria naturally swap with neighbors — and scientists can remove them and get bacteria to take them back up

questions.explanation: A plasmid is a small DNA loop separate from the chromosome with accessory genes; bacteria exchange copies by horizontal gene transfer.

questions.prompt: Why must the primers in a diagnostic PCR test match a sequence found in the pathogen but NOT in human DNA?

options.text: Pathogen DNA is single-stranded, so only it can bind primers
If they matched human DNA, the patient's own DNA would be amplified and every test would come back positive
Human DNA can't be denatured at 96 °C, so the primers would never find it
If they matched human DNA, Taq polymerase would be destroyed by human enzymes

questions.explanation: A positive result means the primer-targeted sequence was present and amplified. The target must be unique to the microbe.

questions.prompt: The COVID PCR test is an RT-PCR. Why is the reverse transcriptase step needed?

options.text: Reverse transcriptase replaces Taq polymerase, which can't survive the 96 °C step
Reverse transcriptase destroys human DNA so only viral DNA is left in the tube
SARS-CoV-2 has an RNA genome, and reverse transcriptase makes a DNA copy that DNA polymerase can then amplify
SARS-CoV-2 has a DNA genome that must be turned into RNA before the primers can bind

questions.explanation: Reverse transcriptase makes DNA from an RNA template. PCR's DNA polymerase copies DNA. SARS-CoV-2's genome is RNA.

questions.prompt: When Cas9 cuts a gene, why usually can't the cell repair it by copying its homologous chromosome?

options.text: Human cells are haploid, like bacteria, so there is never a homologous chromosome to copy from in the first place
Cas9 probably finds and cuts the same target on both homologous chromosomes, so there is no intact copy to copy from
Homology-directed repair only works on RNA, so it can repair the guide RNA but not the cut chromosome
Cas9 stays clamped to the cut site and permanently blocks DNA polymerase from reaching the broken ends

questions.explanation: Lecture: Cas9 'would actually cut both chromosomes,' so scientists supply donor DNA whose ends match the cut to direct repair.

questions.prompt: Liu You's lung-cancer treatment and Victoria Gray's sickle cell treatment share what key feature that a CRISPR treatment for cystic fibrosis lacks?

options.text: The cells to be edited (T cells, blood-forming cells) could be removed, edited outside the body, and put back; CF would require editing cells throughout the airways inside the body
Both diseases are caused by viruses whose DNA Cas9 can cut out of the cells, while CF is caused by a bacterial infection of the lungs
Both used non-homologous end joining to knock genes out, while CF needs a knock-in that has never worked in human cells
Both were done on embryos before birth, so every cell inherited the fix, while CF can only be treated after symptoms appear in adults

questions.explanation: Removing, editing, and returning cells makes adult treatment feasible. CF affects every cell, so you'd need Cas9 in at least all respiratory cells.

questions.prompt: What attitude did Paul Berg (1970) and Jennifer Doudna (2015) share about new genetic technology?

options.text: Both rushed to be first, announcing results before other labs could repeat the experiment
Neither said 'never' — both said it was too soon to take the next step (putting recombinant DNA in E. coli; editing human embryos)
Both refused to publish their discoveries in journals so the methods couldn't be copied
Both believed the technology was too dangerous ever to use and called for a permanent worldwide ban

questions.explanation: Berg: not never, just not yet. Doudna convened scientists who agreed not to edit human embryos yet.

questions.prompt: How do the two CRISPR strategies for pig-to-human organ transplants differ?

options.text: One knocks out a pig embryo's organ-development genes and adds human stem cells so the organs grow from human cells; the other knocks out the pig genes for antigens our bodies reject
One edits the human patient's T cells so they accept pig tissue; the other edits the pig's DNA polymerase so pig cells copy human genes
One inserts the human insulin gene into pigs so their organs match ours; the other removes the pig CCR5 gene so organs resist HIV
One uses PCR to grow extra copies of a pig's organs in a dish; the other uses restriction enzymes to shrink pig organs to human size

questions.explanation: Jun Wu: pig blastocyst + human stem cells (chimera). Other approach: turn off pig antigen genes — the kidney transplanted into Rick Slayman.

questions.prompt: Why is a PCR reaction cooled from 96 °C to about 55 °C before extension?

options.text: Cooling restarts Taq polymerase, which is inactive above 55 °C and would otherwise never extend the strands
Cooling lets ligase glue the Okazaki fragments from the last cycle together before the next round begins
At 96 °C hydrogen bonds break and strands separate; cooling lets the primers form hydrogen bonds with their complementary sequences (annealing)
Cooling lets the helicase in the tube rebind the DNA and unzip the next region to be copied

questions.explanation: Denaturation (96 °C) breaks H-bonds; annealing (~55 °C) lets primers bind; extension (~72 °C) is when polymerase works.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the history of genetic engineering is FALSE?

options.text: Cohen and Boyer created the first recombinant organism in 1973.
Cohen and Boyer created the first recombinant DNA molecule in 1970.
Boyer and Swanson formed Genentech and produced human insulin in E. coli.
Restriction enzymes were discovered by Smith, Nathans, and Arber (Nobel 1978).
Paul Berg joined DNA from SV40 and lambda phage using a restriction enzyme and ligase.

questions.explanation: False — Paul Berg made the first recombinant DNA (1970). Cohen and Boyer made the first recombinant organism (1973).

questions.prompt: Which statement about the steps of a PCR cycle is FALSE?

options.text: At about 72 °C, the primers anneal to the single strands.
At about 55 °C, the primers bind (anneal) to their complementary sequences.
At about 96 °C, the DNA is denatured into single strands.
The cycle is usually repeated about 25–35 times.
A thermal cycler switches between the temperatures automatically.

questions.explanation: False — 72 °C is extension, when DNA polymerase extends the primers. Annealing is ~55 °C.

questions.prompt: Compare restriction enzymes and Cas9 as tools for cutting DNA. Explain what decides where each one cuts and why Cas9 is more precise and more flexible.
questions.explanation: A restriction enzyme cuts (cleaves) DNA at its own specific short recognition sequence — e.g., EcoRI cuts GAATTC with a staggered cut that leaves sticky ends. That short sequence probably appears many times in a genome, and each enzyme is stuck with its one sequence. Cas9 is an enzyme that cuts DNA wherever its guide RNA's ~20-letter target sequence matches the DNA by complementary base pairing. A 20-letter sequence is unlikely to occur more than once, so the cut is precise, and Cas9 is programmable — swap in a guide RNA with a different target sequence to cut a different gene.

questions.prompt: Explain how CRISPR can be used to knock a gene OUT and to knock a gene IN, and which approach would be needed to treat cystic fibrosis.
questions.explanation: Cas9, guided by its guide RNA, cuts the gene at the target sequence. Knock-out: with no donor DNA, the cell repairs the break by non-homologous end joining, sticking in random nucleotides; the mutation inactivates the gene. Knock-in: scientists add synthetic donor DNA whose ends match the cut site; the cell treats it as the homologous chromosome and uses homology-directed repair to copy the new sequence in. Cystic fibrosis is caused by a faulty CFTR gene that already doesn't work, so cutting it alone doesn't help — it requires knock-in with donor DNA carrying the correct CFTR sequence (as Hans Clevers did in cells in a dish).
